look_here_first: LOOK at actual ROSETTE in USFWS SSA Fig. 2.1a (linked below) for broad, thick, glossy dark-green basal blades. In the installed USFWS close-up, inspect the roughly 4-cm crimson tube with upper/lower corolla lips and green-to-purple calyx; it does NOT photograph the rosette, despite misleading media-page title. Compare cedar sage's smaller crimson blooms and often 1–3 leaflet long-petioled rosette versus scarlet sage's triangular simple leaves up stems.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: perennial herb with persistent basal rosette

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Long-lived perennial with thick basal rootstock and a persistent rosette, one or several flowering stalks to about 1.5 m.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Smooth thick dark-green basal rosette leaves, can be as long as 12 cm; not usually pinnately 1–3-foliolate like some cedar sage.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: Tall unbranched or sparsely branched stiff four-sided flowering stalk with big tubular red to purplish-red blooms.

key_traits.label: Flower dimensions
key_traits.text: Corolla typically around 4 cm tubular, scarlet to reddish purple. Calyx green, becoming purple with age; flower much larger than local cedar sage in typical conditions.

key_traits.label: Habitat
key_traits.text: Typically shaded/seep-moist limestone ravines, bluffs and streamside ledges, within the Edwards Plateau; a rare, conservation-sensitive wild taxon.

key_traits.label: Rare plant caution
key_traits.text: Do not disclose exact locations or collect wild specimens for photographs. USFWS sources indicate at-risk, narrowly distributed native.
